case_study_insert.main_stem: Caldera Springs Spa Resort (CSSR) is a cooperative in the wellness and spa tourism sector, employing a workforce of 65. Founded in 2016 by Priya Raman, the resort operates geothermal baths and a treatment wing in the highlands, with a flat structure and democratic leadership. CSSR plans to invest $950,000 in a new geothermal bath house and treatment suites, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $28 a unit and a selling price of $52, and currently produces 21,000 units a year. CSSR faces two operational problems: labour turnover among therapists has reached 19% and quality complaints about treatment bookings are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — Autumn 2025: A survey of 550 guests found that 61% would pay up to $12 more per session for geothermal treatments, and 47% check a resort's environmental credentials before booking. Average occupancy of treatment rooms is 74%, and the 480 most recent reviews average 4.7 out of 5. Customer complaints fell from 33 to 17 per month. A skills audit shows 22 of 65 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new digital booking system; off-the-job training courses at the highland college cost $800 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Caldera Springs Spa Resort as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $11.90 to $12.61 per hour from April 2026, raising therapist and front-of-house wage bills. (3) Energy prices have risen 14.2% year-on-year and wellness inflation is running at 6.5%, while consumer spending on wellness breaks grew 6.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: CSSR plans to finance its geothermal bath house partly with retained profit. Explain two advantages for CSSR of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of selling assets.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit keeps the resort's productive capacity intact — selling treatment rooms, vehicles or laundry equipment to raise the $350,000 would remove the very assets that generate the 21,000 units a year and the 74% treatment-room occupancy the expansion depends on. Retained profit requires no buyer to be found, no negotiation over price, and no disruption to guest services during the build.

Point 2: Retained profit costs CSSR nothing in interest, repayments or disposal losses, protecting cash flow at a time when it already faces fixed costs of $360,000 a year and a $600,000 ten-year bank loan commitment. Every dollar of retained profit used preserves margin against the 14.2% rise in energy prices, helping CSSR hold the $52 price point and keep the cooperative's members' returns healthy without diluting member ownership the way an external capital raise would.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Caldera Springs Spa Resort and its geothermal expansion decision.

questions.question_text: CSSR is launching its new geothermal bath house. Consider wellness magazine advertising, partnerships with luxury hotels and tour operators, or social media campaigns with wellness influencers. Which should CSSR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Wellness magazine advertising: High-quality placements in wellness and spa magazines would reach an affluent, health-conscious readership and suit CSSR's premium geothermal positioning. However, print lead times are long, readership is ageing, and much of the national circulation falls outside viable travel distance, so cost per confirmed booking could be high for a 65-employee cooperative funding a $950,000 build.

Luxury hotel and tour-operator partnerships: Formal referral agreements with highland hotels and wellness tour operators would place CSSR directly in front of guests already buying premium breaks, matching the 6.1% growth in wellness-break spending and the 61% of 550 surveyed guests willing to pay up to $12 more per session. Partners receive commission, and CSSR gains a steady stream of pre-qualified groups at low fixed cost.

Wellness influencer campaigns: Partnering with credible wellness influencers builds national awareness with strong visual storytelling around geothermal waters, is trackable through booking codes, and suits the 47% of guests who check environmental credentials. Results build slowly, depend on influencer credibility, and may attract one-off curiosity visits rather than committed bookings.

Recommendation: CSSR should choose luxury hotel and tour-operator partnerships. They convert warm, pre-qualified demand into confirmed group bookings, reinforce the 4.7-out-of-5 review base and the $12 premium guests will pay, and keep CSSR's costs variable with success. Wellness magazine advertising is rejected as too slow and poorly targeted for a seasonal launch; influencer campaigns are rejected as too unreliable as the primary channel for a cooperative investing $950,000, and can be layered in later to amplify the partnerships.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to CSSR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CSSR with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CSSR with a well-justified recommendation explaining why magazine advertising and influencers are rejected as the primary channel.

questions.question_text: CSSR's labour turnover among therapists has reached 19%. Explain two benefits for CSSR of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its therapy and treatment team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives CSSR's 65 employees a genuine voice in rotas, treatment protocols and the rollout of the new booking system, satisfying their social and esteem needs (Maslow) and raising job satisfaction. Therapists who help shape the system are more likely to attend reliably and remain committed, directly addressing the 19% turnover and relieving pressure on the flat structure.

Point 2: Involving therapists taps their daily experience to fix booking errors and treatment sequencing, which attacks the quality complaints that are rising. Higher involvement also delivers the on-the-job suggestions needed to bring the 22 of 65 untrained staff up to standard, saving the $800 per employee off-the-job course cost and protecting the 74% treatment-room occupancy while the new bath house is built.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CSSR's labour turnover, booking complaints and training gap.

questions.question_text: CSSR must upskill 22 staff on the new digital booking system. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the highland college. Which should CSSR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training at the resort is directly relevant to CSSR's own booking screens, room assignments and treatment flows, costs nothing in fees, and keeps the 22 staff productive during the 74% occupancy period. Its weaknesses are that senior colleagues lose productive time, there is no formal certificate, and staff may pick up informal workarounds that bypass the error checking the system is meant to enforce.

Off-the-job training: The highland college course at $800 per employee gives structured, certified systems training for all 22 staff, costing $17,600 in total — affordable within a $950,000 expansion budget. Certification supports audit readiness and any future booking-platform accreditation. Drawbacks are the $17,600 fee, staff time away from treatment rooms during busy weeks, and content that is generic rather than specific to CSSR's treatment menus and geothermal scheduling.

Decision: CSSR should choose on-the-job training for the immediate rollout, with a short off-the-job top-up at the college for the three booking-desk leads. On-the-job training is cheapest, system-specific and avoids further loss of treatment capacity while therapist turnover is already 19%; full off-the-job training is rejected because withholding $17,600 and losing 22 staff during a 74%-occupancy season would hurt guest bookings and the 21,000-unit target, and certification can be added later once the system stabilises.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to CSSR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of CSSR.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of CSSR with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and certificate relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CSSR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($52 − $28) = $360,000 ÷ $24 = 15,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 15,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $52 − $28 = $24.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $24.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CSSR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 15,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 21,000 units to confirm the resort is profitably above break-even, with a margin of safety of 6,000 units, informing whether to add twilight sessions in the new bath house.
2. Contribution per unit of $24.00 lets CSSR model the effect of the $12 per session geothermal premium, for example a wellness bundle priced at $48 would cut contribution to $20.00, letting managers judge whether extra sessions would still cover the $360,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $360,000 and contribution per unit helps managers set the occupancy targets used to justify the $600,000 bank loan repayments and to check the new bath house services them before committing the further $350,000 retained profit.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($360,000 ÷ 21,000 units + $28 = $45.14 a unit) to benchmark seasonal performance, identify purchasing waste behind booking errors, and decide whether to renegotiate the $28 variable cost with linen and treatment suppliers amid the 14.2% rise in energy prices.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 15,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $24.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety vs 21,000-unit output; geothermal premium and bundle modelling vs $360,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $950,000 bath house; and unit-cost benchmarking at $45.14 to tackle waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CSSR's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CSSR's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.56 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.69 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.91 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.19 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $105,000 inventories + $90,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $250,000; 2025 = $80,000 + $120,000 + $70,000 = $270,000. Liquidity 2024 = $250,000 ÷ $160,000 = 1.56; 2025 = $270,000 ÷ $160,000 = 1.69. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($250,000 − $105,000) ÷ $160,000 = $145,000 ÷ $160,000 = 0.91; 2025 = ($270,000 − $80,000) ÷ $160,000 = $190,000 ÷ $160,000 = 1.19.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened. The 2025 liquidity figure improved from 1.56 to 1.69, meaning current assets cover current liabilities more comfortably, helped by cash rising from $55,000 to $70,000 and inventories falling from $105,000 to $80,000. The stricter liquidity measure, which excludes inventories, improved from 0.91 to 1.19, so CSSR no longer relies on selling stock to meet short-term debts — critical while it services a $600,000 bank loan and funds a $950,000 geothermal bath house. However, trade receivables rose from $90,000 to $120,000, tying up cash; if hotel partners and tour operators pay late, the stronger ratios could deteriorate quickly. Inventories fell sharply, so linen and treatment supplies for peak weeks should be monitored.

Conclusion: CSSR's financial position has improved. Both the 2024-to-2025 liquidity measures (1.56 to 1.69, and 0.91 to 1.19) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement does not depend on inventory. The main residual risk is rising trade receivables, so CSSR should tighten deposit and settlement terms with hotel partners while proceeding with the geothermal bath house.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether CSSR's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CSSR of expanding its use of geothermal heating for the new bath house and treatment suites.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Geothermal heating matches the preferences of the 61% of 550 surveyed guests willing to pay up to $12 more per session, allowing CSSR to charge a premium that protects its $24.00 contribution per unit even as energy prices rise 14.2%. It also strengthens CSSR's position with the 47% of guests who check environmental credentials, reduces reliance on purchased fuel, and supports the cooperative's sustainability identity and 4.7-out-of-5 review average.

Disadvantage: Geothermal plant and drilling carry high upfront capital and specialist maintenance requirements inside the $950,000 budget, and output can be limited by geological flow. If the system underperforms or needs downtime, treatment rooms cannot be heated reliably, raising the risk of booking complaints and disrupting the 74% occupancy the expansion depends on, while any visible failure would damage the eco-credibility CSSR sells to the 47% credential-checking guests.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CSSR's research data, costs and geothermal expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase to $12.61 per hour, and the 14.2% rise in energy prices will affect CSSR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.0%): If CSSR's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, annual interest rises by about 0.5%, adding roughly $3,000 a year to financing costs and slightly raising the burden above the $360,000 fixed costs. Higher rates may also cool consumer appetite for discretionary wellness breaks, though consumer spending on wellness still grew 6.1%, and CSSR can partly shield itself by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $12.61 per hour): With 65 employees, mainly therapists, cleaners and front-of-house roles, the rise lifts a substantial wage bill. Roughly 40 staff at or near minimum wage, each working about 1,800 hours a year, would see about $12.61 × 1,800 × 6.0% ≈ $1,362 extra a year per worker, or roughly $54,500 across those roles — serious for a cooperative, though CSSR can offset part through productivity gains of about 323 units per worker (21,000 units ÷ 65 staff) and cross-trained multi-skilled teams.

Energy price inflation (14.2%): CSSR's direct energy exposure is materially reduced because its baths are geothermal — pumps rather than purchased heating oil or gas — so the 14.2% rise applies mainly to laundry, kitchens and common areas, roughly $15,000 to $18,000 a year in practice. It still raises supplier and transport costs embedded in the $28 variable cost, and it reinforces the strategic case for geothermal, which competitors without it will face directly.

Conclusion: The 6.0% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It permanently raises the cost of roughly 40 minimum-wage roles by about $54,500 a year regardless of occupancy, directly eroding the margin that justifies the $950,000 bath house, and it cannot be avoided by CSSR's geothermal technology. The 14.2% energy rise is the second most serious risk at roughly $15,000 to $18,000 and is largely shielded by geothermal heating — the very reason CSSR chose it — while the 0.5% interest-rate rise is smallest at about $3,000 and can be managed by fixing the loan rate.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to CSSR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CSSR's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CSSR with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
